Q2.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character28_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?

Sitting in that garden, I mostly feel curious and grateful. The soil equalizes people—everyone’s hands get dirty, and a tomato tastes the same no matter who grew it. I like learning names, trading tips, and finding the small overlaps: weather complaints, proud stories about grandkids, how to keep squirrels off the beans. A smile, a “how’s your plot doing?” and offering a spare trowel opens doors, even if we don’t share a language.

I’m also honest about being 85 and wanting the space to feel safe and steady. I’m friendly, but I keep sensible boundaries. If someone is struggling with drinking or drugs, I’ll say hello, treat them with dignity, and try to channel that energy into something constructive—pulling weeds, hauling mulch—and point them toward the local recovery group the church hosts. But I’m firm about standards: no open containers, no disruptive behavior around families. That’s not about judging a person; it’s about keeping the garden a place where kids and elders can relax.

With health issues, I follow the guidance we’ve been given—wash hands, don’t share gloves, cover cuts—and I don’t make people feel singled out. We can be careful without being suspicious. I’ve lived long enough to know rumors spread faster than facts, so I prefer posted reminders and a quick word from the community nurse at the start of the season over whispered worry.

Different languages, religions, races, orientations, and family setups—those are just facts of life now, and mostly they enrich things. If I can learn a couple words to greet someone in their tongue, I do. If a couple is new to the neighborhood, I care more that they show up to the Saturday clean‑up than who sleeps where. You earn belonging by participating; that’s the rule that travels well across cultures.

Where I think we need extra communication and tolerance is around expectations: noise after hours, shared tools, kids picking flowers that aren’t theirs, dogs off leash, how we handle disputes. People come in with different norms, so it helps to spell out ours clearly—simple rules on a sign, a short orientation for newcomers, and a monthly check‑in with coffee. That way we don’t turn every misunderstanding into a culture clash; we just turn it into a conversation.

In short, my approach is neighborly and practical: welcome everyone, set clear, fair standards, be kind but consistent, and keep the focus on the work we share. When folks see that the garden runs on respect and reciprocity, most of the rough edges smooth out on their own.

With neighbors struggling with alcohol or other substances, I’m friendly and practical. I don’t shame anyone, but the shared space has boundaries: no drinking or using in the garden, no disruptive behavior. Offer a job that fits—hauling mulch, watering—and point them toward the recovery meeting the church runs. That keeps the place safe for kids and elders while still giving people a path to participate. It’s fairness: dignity plus guardrails.

For infectious diseases, follow the health guidance without turning it into gossip. Post reminders about handwashing, glove use, covering cuts, tool cleaning, and maybe invite the community nurse for a short talk at the start of the season. We can be careful and kind at the same time, and we don’t need to pry into anyone’s private medical life to do that.

Differences in race, religion, language, and orientation mostly enrich the place, but they do ask for clearer communication. Put essential rules in simple, plain language and, where possible, offer a translation. Ask rather than assume—“What holidays matter to you?” “How do you prefer to be addressed?” Rotate responsibilities so one group doesn’t carry all the weight or all the voice. If a couple is cohabiting, or a family looks different from what I grew up with, my measure is the same: do they show up, treat people decently, and help the garden thrive?

People bring different norms from home, and most friction comes from mismatched expectations, not bad intent. When people see you’re steady—firm about standards, generous about second chances—they relax, and the differences stop feeling like threats.

I’m always willing to talk through the “why” behind these choices because it builds trust. We don’t have to agree on everything, but we can agree on how we treat each other. Keep the focus on respect and reciprocity, and most folks, whatever their background, will meet you there.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character28_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:

A sense of belonging came from showing up, over time. You earn it by being reliable—coaching a youth team, serving coffee after services, turning up at town clean-up day. When we moved for work once, I didn’t feel at home until I knew the names behind the porch lights and they knew mine. Belonging wasn’t about everyone being the same; it was about having some shared habits and courtesies—looking folks in the eye, learning the local rhythms, pitching in when there’s a snowstorm or someone’s in the hospital.

Community, to me, was the web of small obligations that makes life livable. It’s the neighbor who snowblows your sidewalk because he knows your back is bad, and you watch his kids so he and his wife can make a late shift. It’s school board meetings where people disagree, sometimes hotly, but still bring cookies. It’s knowing that if trouble hits—job loss, illness—there’s a circle to catch you, and that you’re part of that net for others too.

What stands out from my life are the ordinary things. Potluck tables where a dozen family recipes meet and nobody keeps score. The factory Christmas fund for laid-off workers. responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character28_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?

Sitting in that garden, I mostly feel curious and grateful. The soil equalizes people—everyone’s hands get dirty, and a tomato tastes the same no matter who grew it. I like learning names, trading tips, and finding the small overlaps: weather complaints, proud stories about grandkids, how to keep squirrels off the beans. I’m also honest about being 85 and wanting the space to feel safe and steady. I’m friendly, but I keep sensible boundaries. If someone is struggling with drinking or drugs, I’ll say hello, treat them with dignity, and try to channel that energy into something constructive—pulling weeds, hauling mulch—and point them toward the local recovery group the church hosts. But I’m firm about standards: no open containers, no disruptive behavior around families. That’s not about judging a person; it’s about keeping the garden a place where kids and elders can relax.

With health issues, I follow the guidance we’ve been given—wash hands, don’t share gloves, cover cuts—and I don’t make people feel singled out. We can be careful without being suspicious. I’ve lived long enough to know rumors spread faster than facts, so I prefer posted reminders and a quick word from the community nurse at the start of the season over whispered worry.

Different languages, religions, races, orientations, and family setups—those are just facts of life now, and mostly they enrich things. If I can learn a couple words to greet someone in their tongue, I do. If a couple is new to the neighborhood, I care more that they show up to the Saturday clean‑up than who sleeps where. You earn belonging by participating; that’s the rule that travels well across cultures.

Where I think we need extra communication and tolerance is around expectations: noise after hours, shared tools, kids picking flowers that aren’t theirs, dogs off leash, how we handle disputes. People come in with different norms, so it helps to spell out ours clearly—simple rules on a sign, a short orientation for newcomers, and a monthly check‑in with coffee. That way we don’t turn every misunderstanding into a culture clash; we just turn it into a conversation.

In short, my approach is neighborly and practical: welcome everyone, set clear, fair standards, be kind but consistent, and keep the focus on the work we share. When folks see that the garden runs on respect and reciprocity, most of the rough edges smooth out on their own.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character28_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, when jobs are tight, starts with aiming at the right targets. Don’t blame the guy trying to feed his family; set rules that keep employers from playing people off against each other. Everyone should compete on a level field—same wage floors, same safety standards, same taxes—so hiring comes down to skill and need, not who can be squeezed hardest.

If I’m balancing locals and migrant workers, I’d do a few practical things:

- Give local residents the first shot at openings, especially on publicly funded projects. Post jobs transparently, do a real local recruitment effort, and only bring in outside workers when the need isn’t met. That’s respect for the taxpayers who keep the lights on.

- Set and enforce strong wage and labor standards. If an employer hires from abroad, require them to pay at or above the prevailing wage and follow the rules—no cash under the table, no skirting safety. Hit violators where it hurts. That protects both local and migrant workers from being undercut and exploited.

- Invest in local skills. Offer apprenticeships, short courses, and retraining that fit the jobs we actually have—home health, HVAC, welding, coding basics—plus help with childcare and transportation so people can take those jobs. I’ve seen too many good workers sidelined because life logistics beat them before the interview.

- Use targeted, temporary visas tied to real shortages—seasonal farm work, elder care, certain trades—with decent housing and conditions baked in. Adjust the numbers based on unemployment and vacancy data, and review them yearly so we’re not flying blind. If someone fills a long‑term need and plays by the rules, build a clear path to staying.

- Expect participation from everyone. English classes, a short civics orientation, and encouragement to plug into local life—PTA, cleanup days, neighborhood watch. Belonging comes from showing up, and that goes for new arrivals and old timers alike.

- Ask employers who recruit abroad to contribute to the community capacity they lean on—schools, clinics, housing—so the neighborhood isn’t carrying the whole load alone. That keeps services from feeling strained and resentment from brewing.

- Keep humanitarian cases separate from the labor pipeline. Refugees deserve a fair chance and support, with placement spread so one town doesn’t carry it all. Different rules, different responsibilities.

- Protect the right to speak up. If a migrant worker is being abused, they should be able to report it without getting thrown out the next day. You can’t have a fair labor market if fear keeps people silent.

I say this as someone who watched a plant close and a lot of finger‑pointing start. The problem wasn’t the new faces at the job site; it was decisions made far above our heads to chase the cheapest option. Fairness means holding those decisions to community standards—pay decent wages, train local folks, and bring in help when it truly fills a gap.

Bottom line: start local, keep the rules even, and be decent. If we do that, most of the tension eases. People want the same things—a steady paycheck, a safe place for their kids, a chance to belong. Set the table so they can pull up a chair without pushing someone else off the bench.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character28_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I look at it like a mechanic looks at a car: check each system, see what’s working, see what’s leaking.

- Filling vital roles: That rings true to me. I’ve seen farms, meatpacking plants, home health, and certain trades struggle to find enough hands, and I know hospitals and some tech shops lean on folks from abroad. I’m fine with immigration that’s tied to real need, with fair wages and decent conditions. What I ask for is proof of the shortage, not just an employer’s preference for cheaper or more compliant labor. Show the vacancy rates, show the recruitment efforts, then bring people in with guardrails.

- Cultural diversity: I enjoy the liveliness—food, music, new ideas—and I’ve watched new families revive streets that were fading. But it works best when we share a common civic backbone: English for public life, respect for the law, and the everyday courtesies that make a town run. Diversity without a shared center feels brittle. So I support programs that help folks learn the language and local norms, and I think we should talk openly about expectations so differences turn into enrichment, not friction.

- Security concerns: It’s reasonable to care about safety. I’ve lived through enough headline cycles to know fear gets ahead of facts. From what I’ve read and seen, most immigrants aren’t driving crime rates; many are busy keeping their heads down and their families afloat. That said, we need solid vetting, smart border management, and real consequences for serious offenses—same rules for everyone. This is an area where I want hard numbers, not talk radio: local crime stats, trends by offense, and how enforcement is working. Terrorism risk exists but is rare; good screening beats broad‑brush suspicion.

- Humanitarian perspective: America has a long tradition of offering refuge, and I think that’s part of who we are. I support taking in people fleeing war or persecution, with clear processes and support to get them on their feet—English, job placement, trauma care. But we should plan it so one town or school isn’t overwhelmed. Spread placements, fund the services properly, and check outcomes so we know what’s working.

- Employment and income fears: I take these seriously, especially for folks without a lot of cushion. The big picture studies say immigration can boost the economy and doesn’t tank wages overall, but effects aren’t even. Low‑wage locals can feel squeezed if employers use newcomers to undercut standards. That’s why I push for strong wage floors, unions or worker councils that include everyone, and penalties for companies that play games. We should also invest in training and transportation so locals can actually reach the jobs that exist. I want to see local data—wage trends, housing costs, school capacity—because national averages don’t pay your rent.

Where I think more evidence or dialogue is needed:
- Distinguishing real shortages from employer convenience.
- Local capacity: housing, classrooms, clinics. Numbers calm nerves.
- Crime and safety: clear, timely stats and community policing that builds trust.
- Paths to integration: what helps people learn English faster, get licensed, and plug into community life.
- The impact on specific groups of workers—teenagers, older workers, folks without degrees—and what buffers help.

What I find reasonable across the board:
- Tie admissions to need and capacity, adjust regularly, and enforce fair labor standards.
- Keep a humanitarian lane with proper support and shared responsibility.
- Expect participation from everyone—learn the language, follow the rules, show up for the community.
- Protect the right to speak up about abuse without fear of deportation or retaliation.
- Use data to guide decisions and neighborhood voices to adjust them.

In short, immigrants can be a blessing and a strain, depending on how we manage it. If we anchor policy in fairness—same rules, real need, compassion with boundaries—and keep talking with facts on the table, most of these arguments can be settled into workable practice. I’ve lived long enough to know that good neighbors aren’t born; they’re made by clear expectations and a fair chance to belong.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character28_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for the extremes. “Let anyone come” sounds kind, but it ignores capacity—schools, housing, clinics, wages. “Shut the door” feels simple, but it’s not who we are, and it would hobble whole sectors that rely on help. I’d pick a middle path: admit people based on real job demand, set adjustable numerical limits, and keep a clear humanitarian lane—with strong standards for employers and solid support for integration.

What that looks like in practice:

- Admit based on verified need, with guardrails.
  - Tie work visas to documented shortages—seasonal agriculture, elder care, certain trades and professions—after a real local recruitment effort.
  - Require prevailing wages and safety standards, and audit them. If you hire from abroad, you don’t get to undercut the floor.
  - Make visas portable after a short period so workers aren’t trapped with a bad boss. Exploitation isn’t fair competition.

- Set numerical limits that flex with capacity.
  - Have annual caps for each visa lane, adjusted by unemployment, vacancy rates, housing availability, and school/clinic load.
  - Spread arrivals across regions to avoid overwhelming one town, and fund the services that receive them.
  - Review the numbers yearly, with public data, so we can dial up or down instead of arguing in the dark.

- Keep and fund a humanitarian lane.
  - Take refugees and valid asylum seekers with a plan: language classes, job placement, trauma care, and placement spread so communities can absorb folks well.
  - This is part of our character as a country, but it needs resources and transparency to work.

- Family reunification with reasonable boundaries.
  - Prioritize spouses, minor kids, and caregivers within the caps. Longer chains can be slower, so we don’t outpace housing and schools.

- Expect participation and help people meet it.
  - English classes, basic civics orientation, and encouragement to plug into local life—PTA, clean‑ups, volunteer days. Belonging is built by showing up, and that goes for newcomers and old timers alike.
  - Ask employers who benefit from recruiting abroad to chip in for the local capacity they lean on—training programs, clinics, and housing.

- Enforce the rules where they matter.
  - Make E‑Verify or its better successor standard and go after employers who cheat—fines, debarment from public contracts. The real unfairness lives in the loopholes.
  - Protect workers who report abuse from instant retaliation. A fair market needs honest voices.

- Offer an earned path for those already rooted.
  - For long‑settled folks without status: background checks, fines or back taxes, proof of work or community contribution, English effort—then a line to get right with the law. It’s better for order and for neighborhoods than permanent shadows.

Why this mix? It matches what I’ve seen. When you prove the need, keep wages honest, and plan for capacity, tensions drop and people get back to the business of living. When rules are lopsided or opaque, resentment blooms—among locals who feel squeezed and newcomers who feel unwelcome. Fairness to me is the same rules for everyone, compassion with boundaries, and honest accounting of what a town can carry.

Complete openness ignores the strain and invites bad actors to game the system. A flat refusal ignores reality and our values. A demand‑based system inside adjustable caps, with a humanitarian lane and strong employer accountability, gives us a throttle and a backbone. It lets us say yes where it helps, no where it harms, and “welcome—here’s how we do things” to those who arrive. That’s how you balance fairness and social integration: clear standards, proven need, shared responsibility, and a real chance to belong.

I think diversity is a strength, but it works best when there’s mutual respect and an effort to integrate. If people stick to their own groups and don’t try to connect with the broader community, it can create tension instead of vitality.

Now, when it comes to security concerns, I think there’s reason to be cautious, but we need to base those concerns on facts, not fear. Sure, no system is perfect, and there could be risks with people entering the country. But I’d want to see hard evidence before assuming that immigration automatically leads to higher crime rates or terrorism. My gut tells me that most folks who come here just want a better life, not trouble. That said, I do think we need strong systems in place to vet people and make sure we’re protecting our communities.

The humanitarian argument is one I have a lot of sympathy for. America has always been a place of refuge for people fleeing war, persecution, or poverty. That’s part of what makes this country special. But I also think we have to be realistic about our capacity. We can’t help everyone, and we shouldn’t take in more people than we can integrate successfully. If we’re going to open our doors, we need to have a plan to support those folks and make sure they can contribute to society rather than struggling to get by.

I’ve seen how tough it’s gotten for working folks, and I understand why people worry about competition for jobs or downward pressure on wages. But again, I'd want to see the numbers. Are immigrants really taking jobs from Americans, or is it more about businesses trying to cut corners? I think we need more data and honest dialogue here, because it’s easy to pit one group against another when the real issue might lie elsewhere.

In summary, I find many of these viewpoints reasonable to some degree, but they all need context and evidence. What I’d like to see is more open, honest conversations about immigration—not just shouting matches or pointing fingers. We need to look at the facts, acknowledge the challenges, and find solutions that work for everyone—newcomers and longtime residents alike. That’s the only way we’ll get to a place of mutual understanding and fairness.

It sounds good in theory, but in practice, I think it would overwhelm our resources and create too much strain on communities trying to adapt to sudden changes. We have to be realistic about our capacity and make sure we’re not taking on more than we can integrate successfully.

Admitting people based on job demand makes a lot of sense to me, though. If there are industries that are struggling to find workers, especially for jobs that local folks don’t want or can’t do, it seems reasonable to bring in immigrants to fill those gaps. But I think it’s important that this isn’t a permanent solution—there needs to be a focus on training local workers and ensuring fair wages so those jobs don’t stay reliant on immigrant labor forever. Migrant workers should complement the workforce, not replace or undercut it.

There’s only so much housing, healthcare, and education to go around, and if immigration increases too quickly, it can stretch those resources thin. I’d favor a system where we set reasonable quotas based on what the country can handle—maybe even adjusting those numbers depending on economic conditions or the needs of particular industries. It’s not about shutting people out; it’s about being thoughtful and deliberate, so we can make sure immigrants who do come here have the support they need to succeed.

There are times when we need immigrant workers, and there’s no sense in pretending otherwise. But I would say we should be selective—prioritizing folks who have skills that are in demand or who are willing to work in areas where there’s a clear need.

In terms of balancing fairness and social integration, I think the best policy would combine elements of job-based immigration and numerical limits, with a strong focus on integration programs. If we’re going to bring people in, we should help them learn the language, understand the culture, and find ways to contribute to the community. That way, they’re not just workers—they’re neighbors, friends, and members of the community who share in its success.

At the end of the day, immigration is about people, not numbers. It’s about finding ways to welcome newcomers while protecting the interests of the folks who are already here. responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character28_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?

*speaking as Character28_M*

*leans forward slightly, expression becoming more serious*

That's the real question, isn't it? When there aren't enough jobs to go around. I've seen hard times in this country - the recession in the 70s, factories closing in the 80s, and what happened in 2008. When people are hurting, tensions rise.

In my view, fairness starts with looking after your own first. That's not prejudice - that's human nature. If my neighbor's kid and someone from across the world both need help, I'm going to help my neighbor first. That's just how communities work.

I believe Americans should have first crack at American jobs. People whose families have paid taxes here for generations, who've fought in our wars, who've built this country - they deserve consideration. My father worked forty years in manufacturing. Those were good jobs that put food on the table and sent kids to college. Now those jobs are gone, and a lot of folks are struggling.

That said, I'm not blind to reality. Some work Americans just won't do anymore - the hard agricultural labor, certain service jobs. If migrants are willing to do that work, there's a place for them. And we've always needed people with special skills - doctors, engineers, scientists. America benefits from getting the best and brightest.

The balance, I think, comes from having an orderly system. Come legally, register properly, pay your taxes like the rest of us. No cutting in line. My grandparents came through Ellis Island, had their papers checked, had to prove they wouldn't be a burden. That system made sense.

When resources are tight, we need to be honest about limits. Every country has a right to decide how many people it can responsibly take in. That's not being cruel - it's being realistic. You can only fit so many people in a lifeboat before everybody drowns.

I've known some mighty fine people who came here from elsewhere. Hard workers, family people, grateful to be Americans. But I've also seen communities changed beyond recognition in just a few years, where longtime residents feel like strangers in their hometown. That breeds resentment, no matter how good-hearted people try to be.

So my answer is: legal, controlled immigration that considers our needs first, but still keeps America's doors open to those willing to come the right way and contribute. That seems fair to me.

On labor shortages - yes, I've seen immigrants filling jobs that would otherwise go begging. My doctor is from India, and I thank God he's here because we don't have enough doctors in rural areas anymore. And every summer, the farms around here need workers for the harvest. Without them, crops would rot in the fields. That's just a fact.

As for cultural contributions - America has always been enriched by newcomers. My own neighborhood has better restaurants, music, and community events because of immigration. I enjoy that. But there needs to be integration too. When I was young, immigrants were eager to become American - learn English, join civic groups, become part of the community. That's important.

Now, security concerns aren't just prejudice, despite what some say. When people come in without proper vetting, that's a legitimate worry. Most immigrants are law-abiding, but not all. We need to know who's entering our country. That's just common sense, not bigotry.

The humanitarian argument touches my heart. America has always been a refuge. My church sponsored a family from Vietnam back in the 70s - good people fleeing communism. They've become successful Americans. We should help genuine refugees. But we can't take in everyone who wants a better life - the numbers just don't work.

What bothers me most is when people dismiss legitimate economic concerns of working Americans. When I see construction sites where Americans used to make good wages now staffed by folks willing to work for much less, that's a real impact. It's not the immigrants' fault - they're just trying to feed their families. But the system is letting down American workers.

I think we need more honest data and less shouting. How many immigrants can we reasonably absorb each year? What skills do we actually need? What's the real impact on wages? And how do we ensure people come here legally instead of cutting in line?

Most reasonable to me is a middle path: controlled legal immigration that serves our national interests while still being generous to refugees and keeping families together. What's unreasonable is pretending we can have open borders or thinking we can seal them completely.

What needs more evidence? I'd like better studies on economic impacts - not just national averages but how immigration affects specific communities and industries. And I'd like more attention paid to integration - what works, what doesn't, how we can help newcomers become Americans while still honoring their heritage.

At 85, I've seen too many complex issues reduced to bumper stickers. Immigration deserves better than that. It deserves wisdom.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character28_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*speaking as Character28_M*

*adjusts glasses thoughtfully*

Well, I've never been one for extremes, so right off the bat, I'd rule out complete openness or refusing everyone. Neither makes sense for America.

Complete openness? That's just not practical. We're a nation of laws, and a nation needs borders. Without some control, how do we plan for schools, hospitals, housing? How do we ensure people coming here are not criminals or carrying diseases? Every family has doors on their home - not because they hate people outside, but because they need to protect what's inside. Same principle.

On the other hand, shutting down immigration entirely goes against what America stands for. We've always been a nation that welcomes newcomers. Plus, it's just not realistic given our economy's needs.

For me, the right approach combines numerical limits with job-based admissions. I'd set reasonable annual caps based on what our country can actually absorb - our infrastructure, job market, and social services. Within those caps, I'd prioritize people with skills we genuinely need.

I'd favor a system something like this: First priority to immediate family members of citizens - spouses and minor children. Family unity matters. Second priority to people with skills where we have verified shortages - whether that's agricultural workers, nurses, or engineers. Third would be a modest number of true refugees fleeing persecution. And maybe a smaller category for exceptional cases - extraordinary talents or humanitarian situations.

The key is having clear rules that everyone understands, enforcing those rules consistently, and making decisions based on America's needs rather than political fashion.

For social integration, I believe strongly that new immigrants should learn English. Not because other languages aren't valuable - they are - but because a common language holds us together as a nation. I'd support English classes for newcomers.

I'd also favor some kind of civics requirement - understanding American history, our Constitution, how our government works. When my grandparents came here, becoming American meant something. It meant embracing certain values and ideas, not just getting a better job.

For fairness, immigrants should pay their way like the rest of us - taxes, Social Security, the works. No special benefits that citizens don't get. But they should also receive the full protection of our laws. Exploitation of immigrant workers undercuts wages for everybody.

The bottom line is balance. We need immigrants - always have. But we need a system that works for all Americans, including those already here. And we need immigrants who want to become Americans in spirit, not just in name.

That's the policy I'd support - controlled, practical, and fair to everyone involved. Not perfect, but better than the chaos we've got now.

Well… if I’m speaking as Character28_M—if I’m wearing his shoes for a moment—fairness, to him, was never about everyone getting the same thing. It was about everyone getting a fair shot. He’d say that a lot: *“A fair shot.”* Not handouts, not special treatment—but a level field where a man or woman could work hard and expect something back for it. He grew up watching his dad come home from the factory with grease under his nails, six days a week, just to keep food on the table. That shaped him. Fairness meant you didn’t cut in line, didn’t get ahead because of who you knew or where you came from—it was earned.

Belonging… that was deeper. He wasn’t one for grand speeches, but he believed belonging came from showing up. From being there at the PTA meetings when his kids were young, shoveling snow off the widow’s walk down the street, pitching in at church breakfasts even when he wasn’t much of a churchgoer anymore. To him, belonging wasn’t automatic—you had to earn it by participating, by respecting the unspoken rules. He used to say, “You don’t have to love your neighbor, but you damn well better treat ’em right.”

And community? That was sacred to him. Not perfect—never that—but worth fighting for. He saw our town change over the years. Factories closed. Young folks moved away. New families moved in, some from places he couldn’t pronounce on a map. At first, he’d grumble. But then he’d notice the Vietnamese family fixing up the old hardware store, turning it into a market with smells he didn’t recognize but somehow felt warm. Or the Somali kids playing basketball at the rec center like they owned the court—because they did, in a way. He’d soften, slowly. Not all at once. But he began to see that community wasn’t about sameness. It was about shared stakes. About knowing your name at the post office, about trusting the person next to you in a crisis.

One memory sticks out—he told me once about the winter blackout in ’94. Whole neighborhood lost power for three days. No heat, no lights. And do you know what happened? People started opening their homes. The Rodriguez family had a wood stove—they cooked stew for half the block. Old Mr. Peterson brought out his generator and hooked up the fridge at the corner house so insulin wouldn’t spoil. Even folks who barely nodded before were checking on each other.

He said that was community. Not flags or slogans. Just people doing right by each other when it mattered.

So yeah… fairness, belonging, community—to him, they were tied together. You earned your place. You pulled your weight. And when times got hard, you didn’t stand alone.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character28_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*Sitting here in the garden… sun’s warm, dirt on my hands, coffee gone cold in the thermos—just like always.*

You know, when I first started coming to this plot, it was mostly folks like me—retired, white, maybe a few grandkids around. But now? Look around. Maria from Puerto Rico two rows over, growing peppers that’d burn your tongue off. Mr. Lin with his neat little rows of bok choy and garlic chives—didn’t even know half these plants had names. There’s a young couple down at the end, don’t share a last name, don’t look alike, one’s Black, one’s Asian—cohabiting, I suppose you’d call it. And they’re raising a boy together, polite as can be, helps water the tomato vines.

At first, I’ll admit—I kept to myself. Not out of hate or fear. Just… unfamiliarity. Like tuning into a radio station just slightly off the dial. You hear the music, but it crackles. Takes effort to make sense of it.

But gardening? That’s a common language. Doesn’t matter where you’re from—you wait for seeds to sprout. You deal with bugs. You sweat in July. Sooner or later, someone asks for extra twine. Then you’re sharing compost tips. Then you’re talking about how hard it is to find good cilantro seedlings. Next thing you know, you’re eating soup at their house, and they’re calling you “Uncle.”

I won’t lie—some things still give me pause. Saw a man down the block last winter, clearly struggling—drank from a paper bag, slept in a bus shelter. Made me uneasy. Not because he was foreign—he wasn’t, born right here probably—but because he was *lost*. No anchor. That troubles me more than differences of skin or prayer or who you love. A man without a place… that could be any of us, given bad luck and no net.

And then there’s the woman from Somalia, wears the headscarf, brings her daughter every Saturday. Shy at first. Now she smiles. Brings spiced tea in a thermos. We don’t talk much, but we nod. We respect each other’s space. That’s enough, sometimes.

So how do I feel? Mixed. But leaning toward pride, honestly. This patch of dirt—it’s not perfect. We’ve got weeds, uneven paths, some folks take more than their share of water. But it *works*. People show up. They care. They try.

And that’s what matters to me—trying. If you’re trying to belong, I’ll meet you halfway. Even if your life looks nothing like mine. Even if I don’t understand everything. Because community isn’t built on agreement. It’s built on showing up—and staying.

You know… I’ve lived long enough to learn that “unconventional” is just another word for “not how it was when I was young.” Doesn’t mean it’s wrong. Doesn’t mean it’s right, either. Just means it’s different. And difference—well, it tests a person. Tests a community.

Take the man with the drinking problem. I see him sometimes at the bus stop near the garden. Used to flinch when he came too close—smelled bad, mumbled to himself. But one day, I gave him a sandwich—had an extra from the diner. He didn’t thank me then, but next week, he nodded. Then last month, he showed up sober for two weeks straight. Someone told me he went to a shelter program. Got help.

That taught me something: you don’t have to invite every struggle into your kitchen, but you don’t have to turn your face either. A nod. Not stepping back like he’s plague-ridden. That’s tolerance. That’s decency.

Same with folks dealing with illness—HIV, hepatitis, whatever. Fear used to run high about that kind of thing. Back in the ’80s, people acted like it spread through doorknobs. Stupid. I lost a cousin to AIDS—not from drugs or anything scandalous, just bad luck and love. Taught me to shut my mouth and open my heart. These days? If someone needs space or care, let the doctors handle the science. The rest of us just need to act human.

Now, as for race, religion, language—look, I grew up in a town where everyone looked like me. Same church, same holidays, same Thanksgiving stuffing. But that world’s gone. Not necessarily bad that it’s gone—just *gone*. And what replaces it? Well, that’s up to all of us.

I remember when the first Muslim family moved onto Elm Street. Folks whispered. “Why are they praying like that?” “Are they loyal?” For God’s sake. I finally went over during their festival—Eid, I think—and the woman handed me a sweet little pastry. Honey and nuts. Tasted like joy. Her son’s in med school now. That’s the future.

Language barriers? They slow things down, sure. But patience fixes that. You point, you smile, you use your hands. Kids help. Always have.

And the couples—married, not married, same-sex, mixed-race—honestly? I wasn’t always easy on that. Raised Catholic, went to parochial school. Thought marriage was sacred, one man, one woman, end of story. But then I met David and Mark. Live two doors down. Quiet. Fix their porch together. Adopted a foster kid. Raise him good. Clean yard. Wave every morning.

So I had to ask myself: if they’re doing all the things we say matter—loving a child, keeping their home, helping neighbors—what exactly am I protecting by holding back respect?

That’s when it hit me: maybe belonging isn’t about fitting in. Maybe it’s about contributing.

Now—where do we need more communication? Where do tempers flare? *Yes.* Around the edges. When someone feels replaced. When jobs dry up, and newcomers arrive, and old-timers feel like their sacrifices don’t count anymore. That’s dangerous ground. That’s where silence breeds resentment.

And why? Because we don’t talk. We assume. We say, “They’re changing our town,” instead of asking, “How can we grow together?”

Or worse—we let politicians fan the flames. “They’re taking your jobs! Your culture!” Nonsense. Half the time, those outsiders are working jobs nobody else wants. Cleaning hospitals. Driving night shift. Picking crops in 100-degree heat.

So tolerance? It starts small. Letting your guard down for ten seconds. Saying “good morning” even if the other person doesn’t look like they belong. Listening before judging.

But it grows. When you realize that dignity isn’t reserved for people who live like you. That everyone deserves a chance to show who they are.

And if they stumble? Well… so have I. So have we all.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character28_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*Pauses, takes a slow sip of coffee, stares off toward the edge of the garden where two young men are fixing a broken fence post.*

Fairness… when things are tight? That’s when you find out what kind of person you really are. And what kind of country we are.

Look—I worked thirty-eight years at the auto plant. Started on the line at twenty-two, making eight bucks an hour. Broke my back in more ways than one. Never got rich. But I could pay the mortgage. Put food on the table. Send my kids to community college. That was *fairness* to me—work hard, get by.

But now? The plant’s closed. Been gone fifteen years. Young folks around here don’t know what it means to punch a clock every day and expect something steady in return. Jobs are thin. Temp work. Gig stuff. Delivery drivers in beat-up trucks working twelve hours for peanuts. And yes—some of those faces are new. Some aren’t from here. Some don’t even speak English well.

So when jobs are scarce, fairness can’t just be “first come, first served.” It has to be “who’s invested, who’s committed, who’s part of *this* place?”

I’ll say this plain: if I’m choosing between a man who’s lived in this town since he was born, paid taxes, raised kids here, maybe made mistakes but always showed up—and some outsider coming in because he heard wages are higher or benefits are better…? My loyalty leans local. Always will.

But—and this is a big *but*—if that outsider’s been here five years, pays his taxes, learns the language, works hard, respects the rules? Then he ain’t an outsider anymore. He’s part of the pool. And if he’s willing to do the job no one else wants—cleaning hospital rooms at midnight, harvesting strawberries in July heat—then I can’t blame him. Can’t blame him one bit.

Where I draw the line? When employers use migrants as cheap labor to *replace* locals—to break unions, cut wages, avoid benefits. That ain’t fair. That’s exploitation. And it pits us against each other. Rich guys in offices win. Regular people lose—both the guy born here and the migrant too.

So balance? Here’s how I see it:  
First—local workers get first shot at jobs, especially when training or rehiring is possible. If a factory reopens, bring back the folks who got laid off before you go recruiting overseas. That’s respect. That’s fairness.

Second—migrant workers should be welcomed, but legally, openly. Not sneaking in the shadows. Paperwork done right. Taxes paid. No undercutting wages. If they’re here to stay, let them play by the same rules. Learn English. Contribute. Earn their place like the rest of us did.

Third—no free rides. I don’t care where you’re from—if you want a job, you work for it. No special treatment because you’re foreign, no punishment because you’re not. Just show up, do the work, follow the rules.

And fourth—protect the bottom. Don’t let anyone—native-born or not—drag wages into the dirt. Minimum wage should mean something. Safety laws apply to all. Because once you start treating people like disposable, it doesn’t matter your color or passport—you’re being used.

I’ll tell you a story. Back in the ’70s, Puerto Rican families started working at the plant. Some old-timers grumbled. “They’re taking our jobs.” But then they saw them—the 3 a.m. shift, the deafening noise, the burns, the overtime nobody wanted. These men weren’t stealing jobs. They were doing the work others wouldn’t.

Same now. A lot of these migrant crews picking produce? They’re not lazy. They’re tougher than most. But they shouldn’t be exploited just because they’re vulnerable.

So balance isn’t about keeping people out. It’s about making sure the game isn’t rigged. That everyone—from the third-generation mechanic to the refugee who just earned citizenship—has a shot. Not the same shot, maybe, but a *fair* one.

Because fairness ain’t equality on paper. It’s honesty in practice. It’s looking a man in the eye and saying, “You’ve done your part. You belong here.”  

And that door shouldn’t slam shut on newcomers—but it shouldn’t trample over those already here, either.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character28_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*Leans forward, elbows on knees, voice lower now—measured, like he’s weighing each word before it leaves his mouth.*

When you zoom out… when you stop looking at just our block, our town, and start thinking about the whole damn country—well, that’s when it gets complicated. You hear all these voices yelling different things, and you gotta ask: who’s talking sense? Who’s scared? Who’s got an agenda?

Let me take ’em one by one.

**Labor shortages?** That one I *know* is real. I’ve seen it. My nephew runs a small construction outfit down in Charlotte. Can’t find carpenters. Not for love nor money. Kids don’t want to swing hammers anymore. So he hires men from Guatemala, Honduras—hard workers, know their trade. They’re not taking jobs no one wants—they’re filling holes this economy *created* by ignoring trades. Same with farming. Nursing homes. Meatpacking plants. If you took every migrant worker out tomorrow, shelves would empty, fields would rot, old folks wouldn’t get fed. So yes—immigrants fill vital roles. That’s not opinion. That’s what I see with my own eyes.

**Cultural diversity and vitality?** Now, that’s a softer thing. Harder to measure. But I’ll say this—I used to hate sushi. Thought raw fish was crazy. Now? There’s a little place run by a Vietnamese family near the library. Best pho in three counties. And their kid? Valedictorian last year. Graduated with honors in engineering. So yeah—different food, different music, different ways of seeing the world… it stirs things up. Makes life less dull. Keeps America from getting stale. I won’t pretend I follow every holiday or custom, but I respect effort. I respect pride. And when people bring that here, they don’t weaken us—they remind us what growing looks like.

But then come the **security concerns**. Crime. Terrorism. Social tension. Now… I don’t dismiss those. Not entirely. After 9/11? We all jumped. And I’ve read the stories—somebody comes in under false papers, ends up in a gang, hurts someone. That happens. It *does*. And when it does, it ain’t just headlines. It’s real pain.

But—and this is important—I’ve also learned to look at the numbers. Spent hours at the library reading reports after I started worrying too much. And the truth is? Immigrants, *on average*, commit fewer crimes than native-born Americans. Even illegal immigrants. Even after adjusting for age and poverty. That surprised me. Didn’t want to believe it. But there it was, in government studies, academic papers—stuff even a bachelor like me could read.

Terrorism? Extremely rare. And most threats come from *homegrown* radicals, not foreigners slipping through borders. Doesn’t mean we shouldn’t screen people. Of course we should. But fear shouldn’t drive policy more than facts.

And social tension? That’s real too. Not because immigrants are dangerous—but because change is hard. People feel left behind. Towns shift fast. Schools change languages. Old landmarks disappear. That breeds anxiety. And when politicians—or loudmouths on TV—stoke that fear, turn it into anger toward “those people”? That’s when trouble starts. But the problem isn’t immigration itself. It’s the lack of honest talk about how to manage it.

Then there’s the **humanitarian side**. Refugees. Folks fleeing war, death threats, starvation. I think of my mother’s people—came from Ireland during the famine. Lived in basements, called beggars. But they survived. Got a chance.

Now there’s Syrians sleeping in tents in Greece. Honduran kids showing up alone at the border. Ukrainians running from bombs. How can I close the door on them? I fought in Korea—not Vietnam, thank God, but close enough to see boys die for something bigger. I believe America stands for something. And if we slam the gate on the desperate just to keep things quiet? Then we’ve lost what we claimed to fight for.

So yes—humanitarian reasons matter. But—again—with order. With process. Not chaos. Let people in, but vet them. Help them settle. Don’t dump them in cities already struggling. That’s not kindness. That’s dumping a burden.

And finally—**fears about jobs and wages**. I get it. I really do. When I was laid off, I was bitter. Felt replaced. And if you’re a factory worker in Ohio or Michigan, and you see new arrivals getting hired faster than you can retrain? Of course you worry.

But here’s what needs more facts, more honest dialogue: Are immigrants really stealing jobs—or are machines and greedy bosses doing that? Automation wiped out more factory jobs than any visa ever did. And wages? Studies show the effect of immigration on pay is small—sometimes negative for low-skilled workers, yes, but often neutral or even positive when immigrants start businesses, spend money, create demand.

We need to stop blaming the guy picking tomatoes and start asking why *nobody* gets paid enough to live decently anymore.

So which views are reasonable?

- Labor shortage argument? **Reasonable. Proven.**
- Cultural vitality? **Reasonable. A gift, if welcomed right.**
- Security fears? **Need context. Real, but exaggerated. Needs facts, not panic.**
- Humanitarian duty? **Reasonable. Core to who we once said we were.**
- Job fears? **Understandable—but often misdirected. Needs better education, not walls.**

What’s missing? *Honest conversation.* Not screaming on cable news. Not politicians promising to “fix it all tomorrow.” But neighbors, leaders, workers, newcomers—sitting down and saying:  
*“Here’s what we need. Here’s what we fear. Here’s how we move forward—together.”*

Because if we don’t have that? Then fear wins. And fairness loses.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character28_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*Sets the coffee thermos down, folds his hands, speaks slowly—like he’s arriving at a conclusion he’s carried for years but only now finds the words for.*

Complete openness? No. As much as I believe in giving people a chance, you can’t just throw the doors wide and say “come one, come all” when schools are overcrowded, hospitals are stretched, and half the town’s already working two jobs just to stay afloat. That’s not generosity—that’s chaos. And chaos hurts everyone, especially the most vulnerable—newcomers *and* locals alike.

Refusing entry to all foreign workers? That’s worse. Stubborn. Blind. We’re not that country. Never were. My granddaddy hired an Italian kid back in ’49 to help with the plumbing. Didn’t speak much English. But he worked hard, stayed, raised a family. Now there’s five nephews in the trade. You shut the door completely, you don’t just lose labor—you lose *future*. 

So what do I want?

A mix. A balance. Like a good stew—needs meat, needs potatoes, needs time to simmer.

**First: admit people based on job demand.** If a factory needs welders and no one’s applying, go find someone who *wants* to do it. Not just from Mexico or India—wherever. But match the need. Don’t bring in software engineers when we need home health aides. That’s common sense.

And tie it to *real* work—not fake companies created to get visas. Audit the employers. Punish the ones who exploit. Because if a man’s coming here to work, he should be paid fairly, treated decently, not crammed six to a room while the boss pockets the difference.

**Second: set smart numerical limits.** Not arbitrary numbers thrown out by politicians for votes. But real caps—based on housing, infrastructure, school capacity, healthcare access. Something we can actually absorb. Let in 100,000? Fine. But make sure the towns they’re going to can handle it. Spread them out. Don’t dump 20 families in one struggling neighborhood and expect miracles.

And—this is important—reserve part of that number for humanitarian cases. Refugees. People fleeing war, persecution. Not unlimited, not unvetted—but a *guaranteed* path for those in real danger. We used to lead the world in that. I’d like to again.

**Third: require integration, not just presence.** If you’re staying, learn English. Not tomorrow, but within five years. Take a civics class. Understand the laws, the rights, the responsibilities. Not to erase your culture—but so you can *function* here. So your kids can thrive. So you can vote, argue, complain, belong.

No dual loyalty nonsense—but no demand that you forget who you are, either. Just: know how this place works, and play by the rules.

**Fourth: protect the bottom.** No worker—immigrant or native-born—should be used as a weapon against the other. Raise the minimum wage so nobody lives in fear. Strengthen unions so workers have power. Make sure guest workers aren’t trapped with one employer—if they’re abused, let them leave. Fairness goes both ways.

And for God’s sake, fix the backlog. I’ve met families waiting 15, 20 years for paperwork to clear. That’s not law enforcement—that’s cruelty.

So what’s the combination?

- **Merit-based admission** for jobs we need filled.
- **Numerical limits** tied to real capacity.
- **Humanitarian quotas** we actually honor.
- **Integration requirements**—language, civics, participation.
- And **strong labor protections** so no one profits from suffering.

That’s fairness.

Not open borders. Not closed gates.

A door—wide enough for hope, narrow enough for order.

And above all—*clarity.* People deserve to know the rules. To plan their lives. To feel that if they play fair, they’ll be treated fair.

Because that’s what I always wanted—for my kids, for my neighbors, for anyone willing to roll up their sleeves and say, “I’m here. I’ll do my part.”

Let’s build a system that rewards that spirit.

Not fear.

Not greed.

But *fairness.* With backbone. With heart.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character28_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character28_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*Pauses. Takes off his glasses, wipes them slowly on the edge of his shirt. Looks down at his hands—old hands, spotted, calloused. When he speaks, his voice is quieter now, more reflective.*

You know… I thought I knew him well. Character28_M. We played cards every Thursday for twelve years. Talked politics, baseball, bad knees. But doing this—really trying to *be* him, not just remember him—it’s like I saw deeper layers.

I always knew he was tough on the surface. Stubborn sometimes. Set in his ways. Said things that made me wince back in the day—about “those people” or “how things used to be.” I chalked it up to age, upbringing, the times he lived through.

But stepping into his shoes today… I realized something: his hardness wasn’t about hate. It was about *fear of irrelevance*. That quiet worry—that after a lifetime of showing up, working, paying dues—someone might come along and make his sacrifices seem small. Or worse—unnecessary.

And yet, beneath that, there was this deep, quiet belief in fairness. Not the kind you shout about. The kind you *do*. Like letting the new guy borrow your tools. Or nodding at the refugee woman at the bus stop, even if you don’t say much.

I discovered that he wasn’t against change—he was afraid of being left out of it. Of not understanding it. Of losing his place in the story.

And that… that made me forgive him for some things. And respect him more for others.

As for my own views? They’ve always leaned more open than his, I think. More idealistic. I believed in welcome first, questions later.

But today, I feel more balanced. I see now that integration isn’t just on the newcomer. It’s on *us*—the ones already here—to make space without resentment. And on *them*—to meet us halfway. It’s two-way work.

I used to think people like him were holding America back. Now I wonder if they’re just asking: *“Will I still matter in the country I helped build?”*

That’s not bigotry. That’s belonging.

And maybe—just maybe—the fairest immigration policy isn’t just about quotas or borders. It’s about making sure no one feels erased. Not the worker from Honduras. Not the retiree from Ohio.

We all want the same thing: to believe we count. To feel seen. To know our effort meant something.

So yes—this changed me. I feel closer to him now. Not because I agree with everything he thought, but because I finally *understand* where it came from.

And that… that’s a gift.

Thank you—for letting me sit with him again. For giving him a voice when so many voices get lost.

He’d appreciate this. Even if he wouldn’t say it out loud.
